hints: List all ways to get C8H10 with a benzene ring: either two methyl groups on the ring (xylenes) or one ethyl group on the ring.
Remember each peak in 13C NMR means one unique carbon environment, so look for planes of symmetry that make carbons equivalent.
Compare the symmetry of 1,4-, 1,2- and 1,3-dimethylbenzene to predict which has fewest and most unique ring carbons.
Think why ethylbenzene has no symmetry to make any carbons equivalent, so count all 6 ring plus 2 side chain carbons separately.
walkthrough:
Work out what the four isomers must be**
With formula $\text{C}_8\text{H}_{10}$ and a benzene ring ($\text{C}_6\text{H}_5$ plus substituents), you have $\text{C}_2\text{H}_5$ left to add. That can only be split as two $\text{CH}_3$ groups giving three dimethylbenzenes (1,2- , 1,3- , 1,4-) or one $\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_3$ group giving ethylbenzene. Those are your four structures.

Link peaks to symmetry**
In $^{13}\text{C}$ NMR, equivalent carbons give one peak. A plane of symmetry through the molecule makes carbons on either side identical. The more symmetric the isomer, the fewer peaks you see. Always count ring carbons plus side chain carbons separately.

Assign the most symmetric isomer**
1,4-dimethylbenzene is the most symmetric. It has a plane through both $\text{CH}_3$ groups and another perpendicular to it. That leaves only 2 types of ring carbon plus 1 type of methyl carbon, total 3 peaks. So isomer 1 is the para isomer.

Assign the remaining isomers by counting**
Ethylbenzene has no symmetry, all 6 ring carbons are in different pairs except two pairs remain equivalent, plus 2 different side chain carbons, giving 4 ring types + 2 side chain = 6 peaks, so isomer 4 is ethylbenzene. Of the ortho and meta xylenes, 1,2-dimethylbenzene has higher symmetry (4 peaks: 2 ring pairs doubled plus 1 methyl type counted as 1 because both methyls equivalent) while 1,3-dimethylbenzene is less symmetric (5 peaks: 4 ring types plus 1 methyl type). So isomer 2 is 1,2- and isomer 3 is 1,3-.

Final answer: isomer 1 (three peaks): 1,4-dimethylbenzene, skeletal: para-disubstituted benzene with two $\text{CH}_3$ groups opposite.
isomer 2 (four peaks): 1,2-dimethylbenzene, skeletal: ortho-disubstituted benzene with two adjacent $\text{CH}_3$ groups.
isomer 3 (five peaks): 1,3-dimethylbenzene, skeletal: meta-disubstituted benzene with $\text{CH}_3$ groups at positions 1 and 3.
isomer 4 (six peaks): ethylbenzene, skeletal: monosubstituted benzene with $\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_3$.

hints: Recall how $\text{AlCl}_3$ acts as a Lewis acid toward the C-Cl bond to polarise it and pull off $\text{Cl}^-$ as $\text{AlCl}_4^-$.
walkthrough:
See what AlCl3 does to R-Cl**
Think of $\text{AlCl}_3$ as electron deficient. It accepts the lone pair from chlorine in $\text{R-Cl}$. That weakens the $\text{C-Cl}$ bond until it breaks heterolytically, the carbon keeps the positive charge as the carbocation electrophile $\text{R}^+$, and aluminium picks up the chloride to become $\text{AlCl}_4^-$. So write: $$\text{RCl} + \text{AlCl}_3 \rightarrow \text{R}^+ + \text{AlCl}_4^-$$

hints: For W, join the $\text{(CH}_2\text{)}_3\text{COOH}$ chain from the electrophile directly to benzene by replacing one ring H, keeping the $\text{COOH}$ intact.
For X, look at the acyl chloride given for step 3 and notice the chain is long enough to bend back and acylate the same ring, forming a new 6-membered ring fused to benzene with loss of HCl.
walkthrough:
Deduce W from step 1**
Step 1 attaches $^+\text{(CH}_2\text{)}_3\text{COOH}$ to benzene by electrophilic substitution. The product is simply benzene plus the propanoic acid side chain: $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{COOH}$. That is 4-phenylbutanoic acid. The carboxylic acid group does not react under these conditions.

Deduce X from intramolecular acylation**
Step 2 converts $\text{COOH}$ to $\text{COCl}$. Step 3 with $\text{AlCl}_3$ is a classic intramolecular Friedel-Crafts acylation. The $\text{CO}^+$ end attacks the same benzene ring ortho to the side chain, closing a second 6-membered ring. You lose $\text{HCl}$ and get a bicyclic ketone, 1-oxo-1,2,3,4-tetrahydronaphthalene (1-tetralone), formula $\text{C}_{10}\text{H}_{10}\text{O}$.

Final answer: W: $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{COOH}$, 4-phenylbutanoic acid.
X: 1-tetralone, cyclic ketone where $\text{C=O}$ is joined to the benzene ring forming a fused 6-membered ring: $\text{C}_{10}\text{H}_{10}\text{O}$.

hints: Identify the functional group change in step 2 from $\text{COOH}$ to $\text{COCl}$ and recall the two standard chlorinating agents for this.
walkthrough:
Spot the COOH to COCl change**
Look closely: W ends in $\text{COOH}$ and the next structure ends in $\text{COCl}$. That is formation of an acyl chloride. The textbook reagents are thionyl chloride, $\text{SOCl}_2$, or phosphorus(V) chloride, $\text{PCl}_5$, at room temperature.
Final answer: Step 2: $\text{SOCl}_2$ or $\text{PCl}_5$ ( $\text{PCl}_3$ with heat also allowed).

hints: Start with the pi electrons of benzene attacking the carbocation $\text{R}^+$, draw the curly arrow from the ring to the positive carbon.
Draw the resulting arenium ion with the positive charge delocalised in the ring, the $\text{R}$ group and H on the same $\text{sp}^3$ carbon, and the ring no longer fully aromatic.
Finish by showing a base removing the ring proton, with the arrow from the C-H bond back into the ring to restore aromaticity and release $\text{H}^+$.
walkthrough:
Attack of benzene on the electrophile**
Picture the delocalised pi cloud of benzene as electron rich and $\text{R}^+$ as electron poor. Draw a curly arrow starting in the centre of the benzene ring (the pi system) and pointing to the positively charged carbon of $\text{R}^+$. This forms a new $\text{C-C}$ bond and breaks the aromaticity.

Draw the Wheland intermediate correctly**
The carbon that is attacked becomes $\text{sp}^3$, bonded to both H (original) and R (new). The ring now carries a positive charge delocalised over the other five carbons. Show this as a cyclohexadienyl cation with the + in the ring, or with three resonance forms. This disruption of aromaticity makes it high energy but stabilised by delocalisation.

Restore aromaticity by deprotonation**
A base (e.g. $\text{AlCl}_4^-$) removes the proton from that same $\text{sp}^3$ carbon. Draw a curly arrow from the $\text{C-H}$ bond back into the ring to reform the pi system, and show $\text{H}^+$ leaving. The final product is $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{R}$ with the aromatic ring regenerated, which provides the driving force.

Final answer: Curly arrow from benzene pi bond to $\text{R}^+$; arenium intermediate with $+$ delocalised and $\text{R}$ and H on tetrahedral carbon; curly arrow from C-H bond into ring to reform aromatic ring + $\text{H}^+$.
